what_its_for: Bacitracin is an antibiotic used to prevent or treat minor skin infections caused by bacteria. It is commonly used on small cuts, scrapes, and burns to keep them from getting infected. A special injectable form is used in hospitals for serious infections, but most people use the ointment form at home.
how_to_take: For the skin ointment: Clean the affected area gently with mild soap and water, then pat it dry. Apply a thin layer of bacitracin ointment to the cut, scrape, or wound using a clean fingertip or cotton swab. You may cover the area with a bandage if needed. Wash your hands before and after applying the ointment. Do not use this medicine in your eyes, inside your nose, or swallow it.
dosing: For adults and children 2 years and older: Apply a thin layer of ointment to the affected skin area 1 to 3 times per day, or as directed by your doctor or the product label. Do not use on large areas of skin or for more than 7 days unless your doctor tells you to. For children under 2 years old, ask your doctor before using.
missed_dose: If you forget to apply a dose, apply it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular routine. Do not apply extra ointment to make up for a missed application.
storage: Store bacitracin ointment at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not freeze. Keep the cap tightly closed when not in use. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use the ointment past the expiration date printed on the tube.
what_to_avoid: Do not use bacitracin on large areas of your body, deep wounds, puncture wounds, animal bites, or serious burns — see a doctor for those. Avoid getting this medicine in your eyes, ears, mouth, or nose. Do not use if you are allergic to bacitracin. Avoid using other antibiotic ointments on the same area at the same time unless your doctor says it is okay. Do not share your ointment tube with other people.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you notice: a rash, itching, swelling, dizziness, or trouble breathing (these could be signs of a serious allergic reaction); the wound becomes more red, swollen, warm, or painful; you see pus or the wound smells bad; you develop a fever; the wound is not healing after 7 days of treatment; or if your symptoms get worse instead of better. Go to the emergency room if you think you are having a severe allergic reaction.
when_it_works: Bacitracin starts working right away to help prevent bacteria from growing in minor wounds. You should see the wound beginning to heal within a few days. Most minor cuts and scrapes improve within 5 to 7 days of treatment. If you do not see improvement after 7 days, contact your doctor.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Bacitracin skin ointment is generally considered safe to use on small areas of skin during pregnancy and breastfeeding, but always check with your doctor first. Children: Safe for children 2 years and older for minor skin wounds; ask a doctor before using on children under 2. Elderly patients: No special changes are needed for older adults using the ointment form. People with kidney problems: The skin ointment is generally safe for minor use, but the injectable form requires special monitoring by your doctor if you have kidney disease.
